content.text: The text develops Ruskin’s theory of architecture from construction to ornament. Walls consist of foundations, veil, string courses, and cornice; walls may be concentrated into piers and circular columns, whose bases, shafts, and capitals express both actual and perceived security. Arches, voussoirs, tracery, roofs, parapets, brackets, towers, apertures, and buttresses should visibly follow structural necessity rather than affectation. Southern and Northern traditions differ in curves, materials, roofs, and support systems. Ornament should express delight in God’s natural creation—especially abstract lines, crystals, water, animals, vegetation, and leaves—not imitate human manufactures or decorate architecture with miniature architecture. Ornament must remain subordinate to its architectural place and function. Mary went back to the bedroom, moved to the office, and later went back to the bathroom.
